utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear? Very well. Before we proceed with the cross-examination, the cross-examination of Colonel Landry, I would like to turn to the Prosecutor for an organisational matter. For various reasons -- some of which have to do with myself, others with the Tribunal -- there may not be a hearing tomorrow afternoon, which would mean there would not be a hearing. This would mean that we should finish with the cross-examination and the other questions to be asked of Colonel Landry this morning. Does this seem possible, yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is not in my hands because, obviously, the Defence have to cross-examine the witness. I think the estimate that has been given is between two and four hours. If it is four hours, we will not be finished today. I have a number of questions. You and your colleagues will have a number of questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. If I turn to you, it was to ask if you had other witnesses now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have one more witness who we expected to put on tomorrow. I will just confer with my colleague, who is dealing with that witness. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Yes, we have another witness. Your Honours, we have another witness scheduled. The individual we have given notice to, counsel to, is Mr. Ed Vulliamy, who has flown in from the United States. He is a reporter for their Guardian newspaper. He has been here for several days. This is, in fact, his second trip here. We did not get him on the last time for other scheduling reasons. That is the schedule we expected to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will try to work accordingly. Let us have the witness brought in. At the end of the day, we will decide what has to be decided. Let us have the witness brought in and see if we can finish this afternoon. Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can produce the first document I will be showing the witness in a few moments to the Registrar to save a few moments time. (Handed). May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First I would like to say good afternoon to Colonel Landry. Now we can proceed. Go ahead. LIEUTENANT-COLONEL LANDRY (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, good afternoon, Lieutenant-Colonel. You have a collection of documents, some HVO documents, some BiH Army documents, some ECMM documents, which you have kept, as a result of your service in BiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I also have some from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In 1996, investigators from the Prosecutor's Office came and spent a week with you, interviewing you and reviewing that private archive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you say that they spent a week with me, it was not five days in a row, eight hours a day. They were in Montreal for about a week, but they did not -- not all of them saw all of my documents, but only those that they were particularly interested in. When we spoke about a subject, I would show them what I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The last time you and I corresponded in 1997, you said that you would give access to that archive to the Defence but only after you arrived here in The Hague for your testimony. Is that still your wish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my intention, but I have to tell you that I do not have all my documents with me and I have to tell you also that you never answered my letter saying that you wanted all the things I had with me, but simply to have the opinion of my Canadian attorneys. I spoke about more than what you asked with you and afterwards my attorney said to me: "I will see you in court". After that, I had no further news. I do not have all my documents with me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you willing to make them available to the Defence in Montreal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am objecting at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief. This has absolutely nothing to do with the content of the witness's testimony, particularly bearing in mind that we need to actually finish him this afternoon. If we indulge in this type of discussion, this cross-examination will be going on for hours and hours and hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Except, Mr. President, that the documents he produced with his signature on them are from that archive, an archive of a number of bankers' boxes that has never been made available to the Defence. If the Lieutenant-Colonel meant what he said yesterday, that he would be pleased for Colonel Blaskic if he is not guilty, then it is relevant whether or not he is willing to make those documents from available to the Defence. If he is not, the court can draw certain conclusions from that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think there is a rule which has to applied in the context where the cross-examination should remain within the confines of the examination-in-chief. We have established that rule, it can be applied -- it will be applied to your advantage when you bring in your own witnesses, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well, I will move on. I think it was within the scope and it goes to bias. I will move on if that is the court's order. You have a document before you, Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, Mr. Hayman. Decisions are always subjective, you know. You should know that as much as possible, I try to maintain balance, which is complicated. I am not saying that it is completely equal. Try to reformulate your question so that we can remain positive. I can go back partially, if you like. I do not want you to feel at all that I might have in any way prejudiced the rights of General Blaskic. I am simply trying to work in such a way that in the Tribunal, in which if we were to have the Tribunal, hours and hours testifying for so long, we would not be surprised that the trials are so long, lengthy, as well. That is what I am saying and my colleagues as well. That is my -- the decision is subjective. I would ask that you reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will ask one last question in this area, if the court will allow it, I will be done. Will you make those documents available for Defence review on whatever terms you would like to set, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give out the documents the way I did with the attorneys who came to see me. I was there, I would not authorise that. I do not want just to manipulate my documents without my being there, as they are mine. As I did last time, they were documents for a specific period, I showed them to you. Tell me what it is you want. I could not show you all of them, I have at least 50 books. These respect -- it was my six months stay in Bosnia, plus three years of research that I did in the university in order to understand what had happened. I cannot give you all of my research without knowing what it is you are looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have answered my question. You have a document in front of you which has been marked as Defence Exhibit 112. This is an ECMM teletype to regional centres dated 25th April 1993. Would you have received this document in your position as the operations officer at the time in RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I must have received it because I was there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And was it authored by your fellow EC Monitors at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, three of them, I worked them during the time that I was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about provocations and reactions. I would like to read you part of paragraphs 2C of this teletype, then ask you a question or two about it. Paragraph 2C -- Defence Exhibit 112: "In the Croat village Miletici, [grid reference given], five inhabitants were murdered by shoots and knives yesterday. They were all men, aged between approximately 20 and 60. According to eye-witnesses, [appears to be 15] Arabic speaking men, dressed in ordinary uniforms, surrounded the village at 1500 hours on 24th April. Their leader was called Rahmadan, and a few of them had police badges on their shoulders, including a triangle. They demanded the villagers to lay down their arms, which was refused. In the following fight, one of the attackers was shot dead. As a retaliation, the five men were caught, while the other [appears to be either 36 or 56] villagers escaped to a neighbour village. The hands of the five men were tied behind their backs, they seemed to have been tortured or mistreated, whereafter they were murdered, some by shots, some by knives." Then the paragraph continues. Would you agree, Lieutenant-Colonel, that this is an example of a reaction to the death of a soldier, in this case the Arabic soldier, then his fellow soldiers reacting by executing a certain number of villagers; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with the description, since one of my colleagues brought it in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is this a fact-pattern you heard on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it was a common way of responding to provocative incidents that were committed by one or the other sides. You also should not forget that this was 24th April, there was already a great many incidents of provocation. We were really at the summit of the violence which occurred between the two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever told that a similar fact-pattern had occurred in Rotilj, at the time some seven or eight Muslim villagers were, in fact, killed? That is, that a Croat combatant was killed in the course of attempting to disarm the village, and then in an act of retaliation those Muslim villagers were killed? Were you ever told that by any briefing or any resident of that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I was told about Rotilj was that it was not a reaction to -- to the contrary, they were old people, they were women, young people, both boys and girls, who one evening -- when there was an armed group dressed in black which decided to carry out ethnic cleansing. Then after that there was evidence that all the other Muslims had been confined at the edge of the village in Rotilj. If I remember correctly, there was an incident in Rotilj where there was a woman who was raped and then afterwards she was killed with several shots. So I think that both of those incidents might be the same one. I think that there was one -- I do not know whether there was one, it was a provocation, then a reaction, but it does show that there was a lack of control among the Mujehadeen forces that were operating in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 287 could be provided to the witness. I will ask you, Lieutenant-Colonel, a question first: you have told us that there was -- appeared to be a strategy on the part of the HVO to delay implementation of the February 13 1993 orders which we have seen. Was that true regarding the release of detainees and prisoners by both sides, if you could try to answer that question. If you need to refer to paragraph 3.2.3., Exhibit 287, please feel free.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No need to consult it. What I can say is what -- we wanted to tell us about both sides but I can -- there were other things which appeared in the beginning of March when they spoke about Muslim civilians who had been arrested who had been illegitimately detained in the Kaonik prison. That cease-fire involved mostly military prisoners, either Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats -- Bosnian Croats. Yet once again, I never had the authorisation to go to visit the Kaonik prison. Therefore, I had to rely on the people in the Commission, on the reports I received. It would appear at that point, yes, the prisoners had been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the date of this document, Exhibit 287? Do you know when it was generated and by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to look at the rest of the other document. I think that it was -- it was around the middle of March. I said to you yesterday or the day before that the Busovaca Committee met every day and that on occasion the Commission, with the Ambassador and the General Blaskic and others would meet twice a month, so that they might see how things moved forward. I think that this report is one of those that was made at the time of those meetings. It was written in April 1993. I just saw the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You are referring to a hand-written date in the upper right-hand corner with a question mark above it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head). Yes, that is right. In fact, I think that it is my handwriting on the top. Yes, I am the one who wrote that, I have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you drafted the document, itself; the typed portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I participated in it, but you understand that this document was the result of the Commission, as such, which was re-vivified by Mr. Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record and for translation, paragraph 3.2.3 reads: "Order 433, release of prisoners and detainees: joint order has been totally fulfilled." If the ELMO could be activated, please. I would like to ask you, Lieutenant-Colonel, simply for a general reference purposes, indicating where the village of Solakovici is. The map would need to be moved down slightly, if you would like that assistance. If we zoom in just a touch you can see the area. You are indicating with the pointer the village of Solakovici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Solakovici. I have to tell that you as the years have gone by, my understanding of Serbo-Croat has diminished. The names of the villages all sound alike to me. Talking about Solakovici, is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the village of Solakovici, have you found that and indicated that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on map).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you visit Solakovici between January and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, I only arrived in March of 1993. Therefore, I assume that I must have mostly gone to Solakovici around the end of March or around the middle of March. I have to check my notes in order to be sure of the date but from mid-March, perhaps until my departure in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You believe it was between March and August, but you are not able to more specifically identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am asked to be concise and then I am asked to give specific dates, which means I have to look in my notes. I prepared myself, but I did not prepare to answer specific questions -- questions about specific dates and times, I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not need a date and I do not need a time. I was asking for a month. If you cannot recall the month, we will come back to this. You can review your notes during the break and we need not take time now, if that is acceptable to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was there was on 23rd March. I can tell you that -- it is in my notes -- I have two pages of notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, I think that you are right, you cannot answer specifically without looking at your notes, but please try not to get annoyed by the questions. Try to answer. We are asking you to be brief. I have explained why. Having said this, the Tribunal will listen to everything that you have to say. I would just like the response -- the answers match the questions. There is no need to make comments which are really not necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You do not need to apologise, we are all trying to make the Tribunal communicate properly. The Defence slightly altered its questions. Are you satisfied with the answer, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then we can go on. Proceed, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the village between which you have described as "Gornji" and "Donji", Solakovici, were there two sets of trenches facing each other in a parallel manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I thought that I explained last time, that Gornji Solakovici, if I remember, was the upper part of the village on the top of the hill and Donji was the bottom and there was a large field between the two of them and the positions were at the extremities of that field, facing one another. That is the Muslim part was on the top and the Croatian part on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in fact the front-line between the BiH Army and the HVO at the time ran through the village of Solakovici and that those trenches represented trenches on the front-line of the conflict itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is why we were there, in order to have the trenches filled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please answer, Colonel. When you have a very significant comment, make it, but this is simply a question; say "yes", "no" or "do not know". I think that would be better, otherwise you put yourself into a position in which you are going to bring out further questions. It was -- "yes, it was the trench line" or "it was not" or "I do not know". Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You told us of a tragic suicide of an elderly man whom you helped or convinced to cross the front-line in Solakovici. Did he leave a note or make other statements that you are learned of indicating the cause of his tragic suicide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had very close relationship with that couple for about one month. Then I received information from his wife, who, herself, told me that the evening before he committed suicide they had been bombed, shelled. I saw where they were hiding. The door had been ripped off by a shell. The wife told me her husband was extremely upset, did not understand what was going on. On the night of his suicide, he got up at three o'clock -- he got up every night at three o'clock because he had incontinence problems, then he committed suicide. When his wife told me that, nobody else was with me except for the interpreter. That is what happened every time I went to see them, I was never accompanied by any escort, either by the HVO or a Bosnian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have said that in the period March to May of 1993, the tactical situation in Central Bosnia was in favour of the Croats. At the time -- at the beginning of that time period, March, would you agree that the BiH Army had a numerical advantage over the HVO? If so, can you tell us the size of that advantage in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can honestly tell you is that the information that we had at that time was that it was the opposite of March, from what I could see, is that the tactical advantage was definitively on the Croatian side, on the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question was, the number of forces, the number of troops. If you had the information I would be interested in it, if you do not that, is fine, you can tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the time, did Colonel Blaskic's area of responsibility include Zepca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was later on that I learned that there were HVO troops in the Zepca region as well as in the Kakanj region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that at the time, March 1993, Colonel Blaskic's area of responsibility included an enclave that was cut off and isolated, containing Croats and HVO forces in the environs of Zepca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The same was true of an isolated enclave with Croat civilians and HVO forces in the area of Vares; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did there come a time in 1993 when the BiH Army controlled the road running north from Gornji Vakuf towards Central Bosnia and the Lasva Valley? Did there come such a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What dates are you saying, I did not quite get the dates you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did there come a time in 1993 when the road running from Gornji Vakuf to the Lasva Valley and Central Bosnia fell in part under the control of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a time when, on the elevations, not necessarily the village of Gornji Vakuf but the elevated parts, were in fact controlled by the Bosnian troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that by March or April 1993; can you give us a general timeframe or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was much more likely at the end of April or even towards the middle of May. Really towards the middle of May. But I would have to tell you that at the end of 1992, the cities of Vonje Korevokof and Prozor had a Muslim majority, then there was tremendous fighting that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You answered the question. That is enough, thank you. Proceed, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that at the point in time at which the BiH Army held that high portion of the road from Gornji Vakuf into Central Bosnia that any aid or material supplies coming into the Lasva Valley had to -- by road had to first pass through Croatia and Dalmatia, then through HVO territory in Herzegovina, then through BiH Army north of Gornji Vakuf, then finally would come into the Lasva Valley itself; do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with your description because it is not exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What other road routes were available to bring aid or material into the Lasva Valley after the point in time in which the BiH Army gained control of portions of the road running north from Gornji Vakuf into the Lasva Valley? What is the other route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would tell you that some of the elevations were controlled by Gornji Vakuf and Travnik, some of them. Therefore I could not tell you that the area was always under Bosnian control, because that is not what happened, not at all. I told you that possibly after May, some of the elevated points were under the control, but the control which before that had been held by the HVO was no longer as it had been. As concerns the supply routes, we knew that from the very beginning there were three ways for the central troops to supply themselves. It would take some time, your Honour, but I think it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us be clear, Colonel. The question of time is not an abstract and absolute value. Take the time you need to answer. What we do not want is that once you have answered the questions you make comments, unless the comments do appear very important. Do not apologise. Simply answer if you have to. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything that was with weapons that related to the Muslims came from three major sources: the first was the tactical capture. At that time the Muslims, starting in April and May, had a great deal of success in their offences against the Serbs and some of the Croatian regions and captured a great deal of weapons. Secondly, it was an open secret. There was -- in Bosnian -- in Zenica, we were not allowed to go because there were munitions there and specifically mortars that were in Zenica. Third, I had heard that with the checks that had taken place on the roads which gave access to Central Bosnia, in Croatian and HV territory, it was almost impossible to get supplies of arms and other weapons. But I did learn on several occasions that there were convoys, mule convoys that would go through, so I learned that it might be possible for anything that had to do with munitions or other arms could come through the mountain roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the conflict began in January 1993 and continued into April, in the Lasva Valley, when -- at what point did the HVO, if you know, control the most territory? What was the high water mark of HVO territorial control in the Lasva Valley, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was a time when I arrived, as I mentioned. I had been present at -- the Croats had a much more interesting tactical position than those of the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The month of March, the month of March when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree -- here I am going to generally refer for illustrative purposes, not in an attempt to make a specific record, to what I believe is Exhibit 29. Do you agree that as a result of the January 1993 conflict -- a stretch of territory running roughly from Kacuni to the south-west of Busovaca to Bilalovac, which is to the north-west of Kiseljak, that that swathe of land, of territory, came under BiH Army control? Would you agree that that occurred as a result of the January 1993 conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that, as a result of that, the BiH Army Third Corps, which was located on the northern side of that road in and around Zenica and its environs and the BiH Army Fourth Corps, based in Mostar but also present to the west and south-west of Kiseljak, were able to meet up; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is what I said in the beginning when I said there was a group of mountains -- there was a mountain road that went all the way to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just because there may have been a translation problem, I would like to restate the question: would you agree that, as a result of the BiH Army controlling this zone from Kacuni to Bilalovac, that the Third and Fourth Corps of the BiH Army had contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This did occur on occasion, but, at the same time, it would be difficult for me to say this occurred all the time because at that time there was a great deal of combat in the Zenica area. They were very close to Sarajevo and also the Croats were in control of Mostar so, at that particular time, the Bosnian troops were in a sandwich, if you will, between the Serbs and the Croatians. At some point in time it was possible, indeed, to come to contact with the Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Again, there is a slight misunderstanding. I am not asking you whether one could drive from that area of territory between Kacuni and Bilalovac to Mostar. I am asking you, was the Fourth Corps present below the Kiseljak Busovaca road such that they had contact with the Third Corps once that piece of territory was taken by the BiH Army in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have posited the thesis that the HVO provoked, the BiH Army responded, in some -- and I am not asking you to confirm that, I am just framing my question. Yet, you arrived in theatre in March 1993, when the conflict had already begun; correct? January 1993 was the beginning of a war; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would ask my colleague and co-counsel to read the body of Defence Exhibit 88, which is a report from a military policeman in the HVO to the military police in Mostar. My question, so you can be considering it while he is reading this short document, is: did you ever receive this information in your capacity as an EC Monitor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "The command of the Fourth Military Police Brigade of Vitez, on 27th January 1993, writes to the command of the military police in Mostar, to Calic in person." The document is headed, "An extraordinary report". "On 24th January 1993, at 1445 hours, on the main road from Kiseljak to Busovaca, at a locality called Kacuni, fire was opened from small arms on members of the military police from Busovaca. A member of the military police, Ivica Petrovic. "The same person was on that occasion killed, together with another civilian, who was with him. Fire was opened by Muslim forces and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Both persons were massacred and knifed. On 25th January 1993 the conflict spread to the whole area of Busovaca municipality. "We have received reports that the deputy commander of the first companies around Ljubicicic was injured in conflicts with Muslim extremists. We were unable to transport him to hospital, so he may have passed away. The conflicts continue. The commander, Pasko Ljubicicic -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In connection with the commencement of the January 1993 conflict in Busovaca, were you ever given, in substance, that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me the same question yesterday. I told you that when I arrived in March, I did not see these reports but I had heard about certain incidents dealing with the Muslims and the Croatians and that an interpreter from Busovaca had told me this story but I do not have the details that you just related, I never saw this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This document was produced by you, yourself, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This was shown to a prior witness. It is a Defence exhibit. It has not yet been admitted, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It has not been tendered; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Again, with respect to your provocation/reaction thesis, let me ask you about some additional events and ask if you were given the information and if you considered them in connection with your thesis. I would ask my colleague, again, to read only the introductory paragraphs of Defence Exhibit 94, as the rest of the document is largely lists of peoples names and the list need not be read. If you could read -- again, this is a document from a military policeman to military police Mostar and Operative Zone Central Bosnia, Vitez. If you read the title, the first paragraph, then describe the list of 15, then what the heading is before the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The document is dated 29th January 1993. The report is addressed to the police headquarters in Mostar and the command at Vitez. In the preamble it says: "Through operative work in the municipality of Zenica and in the villages of Lasva, Dusina and Visjnica and on the basis of statements of numerous witnesses of an unheard of crime against Croats, who in the mentioned villages of the Zenica municipality, which were committed by Muslim extremists in these villages, it has been established without any doubt that the following have been killed." Now we have 15 names, mostly last name Kegelj. Then there are the names of 29 people taken to prison and eight people who are missing, listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn of events in the villages Lasva, Dusina and Visnjica in the end of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not recall having seen or received anything during this period when I arrived. I must reiterate what I said before, I heard certain things, but I received no report. These reports were not sent to the ECMM. The only report that the ECMM received, and, in fact, I can produce these if you wish, were always addressed to the headquarters of the ECMM. The practice that was very commonplace is that each time a protest was issued, both sides received a copy of these protests, that way both sides could investigate on their own accord. Indeed, there were stories on both sides, both quite horrible. The way we ourselves could try to demystify what was true and what was false was, indeed, to investigate together. I am not trying to be disrespectful towards the Defence, he can list as many documents as he wishes, but I would not have seen any documents produced before the month of March. I began to work in March with documents presented to me. I do not know about documents that may have been produced in February. I believe that there were perhaps errors on both sides and perhaps it was the Muslims that began, that is a possibility as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you say that your interpreter lost family members in the January 1993 conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Two members, two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were those Croat or Muslim victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were Croatian Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Without identifying the interpreters, if you look at Defence Exhibit 94, which is before you, do you see the surname of your interpreter -- of that person's family on the exhibit, if you look on the first page, numbers 1 to 15, indicating the dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, all I know is the name -- the first name of the interpreter. I can bring you to the site in the field but I only know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. One last question concerning January: were you briefed, did you learn anything concerning what happened to the Croat villages, such as Gusti Grab and Oseliste, which were located between Kacuni and Bilalovac in the area taken by the BiH Army; did you learn about those things or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names do not mean anything to me. The first thing I did when I arrived there was to look at all the events that had taken place and all the roads. Indeed, I saw there were indeed houses that had been burnt. But as far as the names of the villages, the names of the list you listed for me, they mean nothing to me, I really do not recognise them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say you saw houses that had been burnt, you are referring to Kacuni and Bilalovac? Did it include that terrain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it did include that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us turn to your visit to Travnik in April, on or about 12th or 13th April 1993. Was Colonel Blaskic present on that occasion in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I remember quite well is that at that particular time, we had been received by HVO representatives in Vitez and all of the Monitors from Zenica from the ECMM were present, so I myself was present. In the end of the afternoon we received information about the catastrophe which had occurred and a few Monitors and a few vehicles went to Travnik to find out happened there. At that moment I must admit -- the day on which Easter was celebrated, I think it was 12th or 13th April, I believe, that they already reported that in Travnik there had been some protests and this had started around 8th April and that even around 8th April, I believe there were already some people who had been killed. I think there were two Bosnian Muslim soldiers who had been killed. All I can tell you is I think around the 12th or 13th, following the Easter celebrations, that I heard about the fact that there was unrest in that area, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand you left the Easter dinner with other Monitors and went to Travnik. Did Colonel Blaskic go with you or to your knowledge did he stay in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. All I know is that I received very specific instructions from Mr. Thebault, but I do not know exactly with whom he was dialoguing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you got to Travnik, did you meet with a representative of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can remember about these incidents is that we met with military authorities there, on that location, and at that time I was convinced that the military authorities there in that location were cooperating and one or two cooperated. I encountered with some of the civilian authorities and it was at that time that I learned that some of the Muslims were being pushed out of this municipality and, indeed, this is what provoked a series of incidents and at that time in the city of Travnik, that there was a civil war under way and that people were raising barricades everywhere and, as I said before, it was indirectly -- the situation seemed to have calmed down when the BritBat forces from UNPROFOR sent some vehicles there to get an idea of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can cut to the quick. Let me ask you if the following statement, which you made on page 4 of your statement to the OTP investigators, is correct, referring to 13th April 1993 in Travnik in the late afternoon: "We met the local authorities of both sides and tried to calm down everyone. One of the authorities I met that evening in Travnik was Dario Kordic, who seemed to be the highest authority on the HVO side." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said there was a civil war in Travnik. Did Travnik -- was it taken control of by the BiH Army in early June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, much later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And were there about 10,000 Croat refugees that left Travnik as a result of that incident, or do you know? If you do not know I am not asking you to look. I am just asking if you have a current recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have some memory, but it is quite a long story. At that time I had a mission -- Mr. Thebault himself reported a two-page document on that incident. If the Defence counsel wishes, I can present this document which will explain exactly the incident at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I think that Defence counsel simply asked you the question to see whether you know about it or not. You can say whether you were aware or not. Is that the question you asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will move on if he has no personal knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You told us of the kidnapping of the four HVO officers on or about 12th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the kidnapping of HVO Brigade Commander Todic on the 15th. Did you learn that on the intervening day, 14th April, there was an assassination attempt on -- on the commander of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic. Is that information that came to you as the operations commander at RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must admit that on 15th April, I was not the head of the operations, I was still under the Busovaca Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My mistake. This was 14th April. Did you come by that information on that day, or do you have no knowledge of it? You are shaking your head side to side --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In connection with the subsequent exchange of prisoners, you have referenced certain Mujehadeen fighters imprisoned in the Kaonik prison. Would you agree that most nations have criminal laws forbidding citizens of other nations from entering the country and bearing arms; that is, foreign nationals from entering the territory of one country bearing arms? Do most countries have laws criminalising that activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure that you are completely right, yes. There are, indeed, laws, that indeed prevent someone from moving about with weapons, but I must also add that everyone had weapons in Central Bosnia. Only people from ECMM, which did not have arms, which were moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you learned, in fact, in the course of your work, that the BiH Army denied giving any authority or permission to these Mujehadeen fighters to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina with arms; correct? They did not give them such permission; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you are right. Later on, indeed, that is what happened. That is what I was told, because eventually Bosnians told us that it seemed that the Mujehadeen activities were more and more violent and that they should do everything they could to try to move away from them and try to do the best they could to return to the area. It is difficult to say, of course, at that time, whether or not they were under the control of Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of these Mujehadeen fighters possessed any explosives or other weapons other than firearms at the time they were arrested and imprisoned in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the story I can recall, these people have vehicles and had lots of money with them. This is the part of the story I can remember, because at no point in time when the stops were made, did the request for the intervention of UNPROFOR which should have been done at that time, or at least for ECMM to see what was going on. It was this aspect which I am finding with this capture of these prisoners to be a bit suspicious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you concede that the February 13 1993 joint orders from Colonel Blaskic and General Hadzihuseinovic did not require the release of prisoners held due to violation of applicable national laws; that there was an exception in the order for persons who had violated criminal laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must admit that you have lost me there in this discussion with international law and all I can tell you is that what I was able to establish was that there were two belligerent forces and I was trying to calm those forces and at no time was such an argument presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: These two sets of prisoners or detainees were exchanged later in May of 1993. With respect to the HVO prisoners, the four officers from Travnik, Novi Travnik and commander Todic, were they held at a secret location by the Mujehadeen fighters, such that ECMM and the Red Cross did not have access to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, would you agree, as stated in Exhibit 290, that the Mujehadeen's demand was, in the last sentence: "They wanted all detained foreigners held by the HVO to be released, otherwise they would start to kill the hostages." Did they make such a demand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, at the actual exchange, you were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The prisoner exchange took place in three locations, Zenica at the Kaonik prison and I believe in Travnik or Novi Travnik. I personally was present in Zenica, I was the one co-ordinating the operation in that location in Zenica, so I was the person who facilitated, in very difficult conditions, I must admit, the freeing of the HVO brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that approximately 100 Mujehadeen fighters appeared at the hotel in Zenica for this exchange, as set forth in Exhibit 290?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not 100 soldiers, 100 Mujehadeen combatant forces. There were many people dressed as Mujehadeen, but they were Bosnians dressed -- Bosnian troops, if you will, but from a Muslim brigade. I have photographs, if you wish to see the troops. I took photographs because it would be quite clear you can see the distinction between the Mujehadeen and the Muslim brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. My apologies for not making that distinction properly. You would agree with paragraph 24 of Exhibit 290, I take it, that: "At Zenica ... about 100 masked and heavily armed soldiers (probably members of the 7th Muslim Brigade) surrounded the place deploying also a three-barrel 20 mm (?) Machine-gun mounted on a 5 TO (probably tonne) truck, shoulder-launched anti-tank and anti-aircraft missiles. "A crowd of some 100 people cheered prisoners when they left the UNPROFOR armed carriers that brought them into the town. They were then escorted from the spot by the masked soldiers who fired their guns into the air when they left." Would you agree with that description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am the one who wrote it, yes. That is what happened. As I stated, it was very dangerous. I was the one of the only persons from the Mission at that point in time who was able to go to that location and to ensure that no violence was committed against the General and I was the one -- and I realise, rather, that this exchange would take a long time, even at the risk of my own life. I wanted to make sure nothing was to happen to the General of this HVO brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were the persons responsible, behind these kidnappings of Todic and the four officers, and the execution-style killing of the four men with Todic, were they ever identified, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they were, through the UNPROFOR intelligence session, because I have one or two pictures which I took which show the Algerian with whom I had negotiated and who said he was the instigator of the hostage taking, mainly having to do with the violence against the HVO brigadier-general in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was any action taken? Was this person detained, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. No idea. All I can say is that we drafted a report. I submitted my photographs to the UNPROFOR authorities. After that I really cannot say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With respect to whatever atrocities or other improper acts took place against Croat victims, whether in Dusina, Lasva, Gusti Grab, with respect to the Todic kidnapping, were you ever given a report by the BiH Army indicating that they had looked into or investigated any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a clear recollection of having seen instructions, among other things in order to limit the looting which seemed to be a common thing in all the villages. I also remember that at no time was there a lack of cooperation on the part of the Bosnians when we were told that crimes had been committed. That is why I can, without any difficulty, say to you that even in August, with Father Stefan, who escorted the Bosnian authorities, we went back to the Bosnian villages that had been evacuated during the April incidents around Zenica. For me, that was enough. I could see that on the ground there was goodwill. There were directives that had been given in order to reduce to a minimum this type of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So, in and around Zenica, you have described and the ECMM teletype describes the deaths of some 15 or so Croats, burning of perhaps 50 houses, looting of perhaps 100 house, displacement of hundreds and hundreds of people. Your view was that there was no need for an investigation by the BiH Army because ECMM's Mission was forward-looking, focusing on protecting those who were alive and protecting things. You were not a law enforcement agency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to do whatever we could do. We had full days but we could not do everything. We worked a great deal with the Red Cross, with the UNHCR and other humanitarian organisations, but since you are raising this point, I do remember in August we received a complaint stating that there may have been -- that there were civilians or Croatians who had been buried. There was a mass grave burial ground. After having received that complaint, I decided with Father Stefan, with the Bosnian authorities to go there. We did not attribute a great deal of importance to this in light of the degree of truth in respect of any unilateral investigation carried out either by the Bosnians or Croats. I wanted to be there and see for myself and see if there was anything that should be added from the other side in order to add credibility to what the other side was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than what you have described, did you receive any reports from the BiH Army concerning any Croat deaths or the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. I cannot say yes, I cannot say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: None that you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us turn to 16th April 1993. You have told us your notes reflect that you attempted to reach Colonel Blaskic and was told, in substance, he was not available; do you have any present recollection of that event, as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In light of the fact that this goes back more than five years, I do have recollection, as I told you. I remember the morning's activities; I remember that I saw the burnt village; I heard shelling, it went on all day long around the British camp. I would have to go back to my notes, because I took personal notes and working notes, which appear in my notebooks. Afterwards, I drafted a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am afraid you misunderstood my question. It was: with respect to the entry in your notes that you attempted to reach Colonel Blaskic on 16th April 1993, do you have an independent recollection of that event, or do you simply have your notes today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could tell you that my records are based on my recollection). If it is noted in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that is clear. The question was asked; you answered; you only remember by consulting your personal log.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards General Blaskic, yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Directing your attention to your observations on that day, the day of Ahmici, you said you saw no evidence of any defence of the village; do you know whether there was a BiH Army unit based in Ahmici, or resident in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether that unit had a plan of defence for the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness has answered that he does not know. Like my colleague here, I am reacting also. Do not ask trick questions, please. You said all questions were subjective, Mr. Hayman. That is what you said, remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will forego the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you saw no HVO soldiers or combatants in Ahmici on the night of 16th April, when you came back or made another pass by. Did you stay on the road in the evening or did you leave the road and go up into the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I did not write everything that I saw down in my notebook. What I did say is that I got rather close to the village of Ahmici in order to have a very, very clear image of the mosque that had been split into two and everything was burning around it. I do not remember that I saw HVO soldiers in the Ahmici village. What I do remember later on is that I have a very clear recollection of bodies lying on the road, when we continued driving through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So, did you leave the Vitez/Busovaca road that evening or did you stay on the road and make your observations from the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to be able to answer the question, I would have to go back to the place physically in order to see that. From that road I could see the mosque burning, as I said. As I said to you, I have a very specific image in my mind of the mosque. Whether you could see it from the road or the main road, I am not sure, I would have to go and see again. I am sorry, that is all I remember right now. I recall the burning mosque and that was very close by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now take a 15 to 20 minute break, which will allow everyone to rest a bit. That includes the witness as well. (4.10 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in again. (The accused entered court) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, the evening of 16th April, 1993, can you tell us whether a front-line had formed north of the village of Ahmici between the HVO and the BiH Army and, if so, approximately where? Feel free to use the ELMO to your right, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where the front was at that time. I have absolutely no idea. It was only a few days later that I learned that -- it was either the next day or the day after that -- the front-line was on the elevation between Zenica and Vitez. That is the only information I had at that point, because you could not go on site, oneself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, the village of Poculica was a BiH army village; correct? If you would like to refer to the map, feel free. Poculica is on the mountain road from Vitez to Zenica, about 60 per cent of the way towards Vitez from Zenica. More like 70 per cent of the way. To the north-east of Sivrino Selo and directly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw it on the map when I was investigating atrocities committed by the Croats, I think that I went there or was near there. I suppose that it was the no-man's-land between the two factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. On the night of the 16th, you returned to Zenica; is that correct, ultimately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you briefed or do you remember anything about events in Zenica on the 15th, other than the Todic kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said at some point the HVO brigade in Zenica was attacked by the BiH Army. Do you know when that was? You mentioned, I believe, the 17th or 18th in your testimony. Can you give us any more precise time on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe you said that on the night of the 16th, you could see certain villages from your hotel. Is that correct? If so, can you tell us what villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think it was the night of the 16th. I think on the night of the 16th -- let me check my notes. Give me a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While you are looking, perhaps Exhibit 292 could be made available to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not the 16th, it was the morning of the 17th, when I woke up and I saw that there had, in fact, been fighting in the general direction that I had just mentioned to you and I saw a column of Muslims all along the mountains in the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were in Zenica; correct, on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Sorry, where was the column of -- I take it Muslim soldiers or do you mean Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslim civilians, who were coming -- who were leaving the combat zone and moving towards Zenica. They were entering the city of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is what your notes reflect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, if you would like to read them. They are in French, yes. Here they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, please do not make comments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not doing it in order to be nasty, I was just trying to cooperate with the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could put your notes aside and turn to Exhibit 292, which I believe has been made available to you. It is the protest, the concern expressed by Colonel Blaskic concerning treatment of Croats in Zenica and the villages around Zenica. You will note that the time of the document is 1.15 am on the morning of 18th April 1993. Would you agree that, at the time, rumours were rife concerning the scale and nature of the conflict that was going on, including in and around Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean whether there were rumours during the day of the 18th? Are you talking about rumours? What rumours are you talking about? I am not sure I got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question: would you agree that at the end of the day on the 17th and the night of the 17th to 18th April 1993, there was a lot of information, including some miss-information in the form of rumours, concerning what was being attacked, who was being attacked, how many people had been killed on both sides, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you also agree that, at the time, Colonel Blaskic did not have the ability to undertake his own investigation of the Croat villages in and around, including to the west, of Zenica. That was BiH Army-controlled territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Later, on the 18th April 1993, you met with General Merdan, you have described. If Exhibit 294 could be made available to the witness. It contains certain minutes from that meeting, specifically paragraphs 4 and 6. (Handed). I would like to ask you about a comment in paragraph 4, titled "political assessment ": "According to the D commander" -- presumably that is "deputy commander" -- "of Third BiH Corps, this" -- which has an antecedent in the document which will become clear I think -- "seems to be part of a master plot against the Muslims from the extremist Croat movement. They have proof that Mr. Kordic had seen the Serb leader, Mr. Karadzic, and they may have discussed the future of BiH." My question is: at your meeting with General Merdan, did he provide any proof or evidence of such a meeting between Mr. Kordic and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the only thing I remember was the content of the sentence here in the paragraph. I think they -- had we wanted to go further we might have found that proof but I did not get any direct proof, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Also on the 18th, you received the cease-fire order from Colonel Blaskic which is Exhibit 293. Perhaps that should be placed before the witness so that he can have it clearly in mind. (Handed). Do you have Exhibit 293 in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question is: did General Hadzihuseinovic issue a comparable cease-fire order to his troops at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to check with my papers. I do not think so. I do not think it was at the same time. I do not think we got it exactly the same time. All I remember now is that there were directives issued in order to ensure the safety of the Croatian civilians. No, I cannot tell you whether I received anything of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did you receive such an order from General Hadzihuseinovic prior to the joint order by Generals Petkovic and Halilovic which was issued on 20th April 1993, and which included a cease-fire order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. I would have to check. I would have to check. I do not have a recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You testified concerning whether the HVO cooperated in an investigation into the events in Ahmici. Let me ask you, first: at the meeting in Zenica, on 20th April 1993, attended by General Hadzihuseinovic, General Petkovic, Colonel Blaskic, Ambassador Thebault, and you were present, I believe, during portions of the meeting, was there any request -- general or specific -- made for an investigation into the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I was only a partial observer because at that point I was working in the operations office, whereas that meeting had taken place in the meeting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any request, ever, by Ambassador Thebault of Colonel Blaskic that he undertake a specific investigation into events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you. I do not remember. I cannot remember whether this took place or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of Colonel Stewart of BritBat did ask -- indeed demand -- that Colonel Blaskic commence an investigation? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that, but I do remember that the BritBat commander did decide to investigate himself. Now, I do not know whether he did this with the HVO authorities helping, I do not know. What I do remember very well is that when we went to visit Ahmici, with the BritBat commander, that was -- the visit was made in armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you been informed that Colonel Blaskic, indeed, ordered an investigation into the events in Ahmici and the Prosecution has a copy of that order? Did you know that prior to or during your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember whether I saw that type of order. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us turn to your April 25th 1993 visit to the village of Rotilj. If Exhibit 298 could be provided to the witness. I will describe my question, then feel free to refer to the document if helpful. (Handed). On page 2 of the teletype which you drafted, there are comments concerning some 600 inhabitants of the village living in a particular part of the village, I believe it is the part further away from Kiseljak than the portions of the village that are closer to Kiseljak. Do you see those references?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you visit that other portion of the village containing the supposed 600 or so residents, or was that information relayed to you by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was information which was relayed to us. As you can see, there were two of us, there was myself and there was Dimitrios Dagos, who, at the time, was Chief of Operations. The day -- it was late in the day and we went forward a little bit to see whether there were any people there, but we did not investigate any more. If I remember correctly, we contacted UNHCR and the doctors at the borders to see if we could bring any medical assistance that had been asked for. Then a report was to be drafted, then my colleague was supposed to take the measures which might eventually normalise the situation with the HVO authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, you have answered my question. With respect to the "convoy of joy" or the "Tuzla convoy", did you witness any events in connection with attacks on that convoy personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I saw were the -- was the results. I can tell you that throughout these misadventures, or the saga of that convoy, I was in the operations room. I am the one who co-ordinated all the activities of all the detachments that were monitoring what was going on. I could not be in two places at the same time. I was absolutely limited to my office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say you saw the results, do you mean you saw the convoy pass through Zenica, or you heard reports in your capacity as the operations officer of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not express myself well. At the time of the convoy I was in my office. I would receive the reports from our detachments. After that, especially in the Nova Bila and Vitez region, I was then in a position to see some of the vehicles that had been destroyed and some of the places where it was clear that there had been rather serious clashes between the people who had tried to hijack the convoy and the people in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that the HVO guaranteed the security of this convoy. Do you know who in the HVO guaranteed this security and to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not have those details in mind. What I do remember very clearly was that the Second Corps authority and the HVO authorities of the Tuzla region came to see us, expressed their ideas to Mr. Thebault and then subsequently with that information, I believe that the HVO representative went to see the HVO representatives in Vitez, since their communications with the major HVO headquarters of the Mostar region was excellent, they made arrangements. Then Mr. Thebault just told me that the local authorities had accepted to -- had agreed to escort the convoy and to ensure its safety throughout the journey. If it was Muslim region, it would be the Muslims who would be in charge. If it was HVO region then the HVO would be in charge. It was always being escorted by ECMM detachments with some UNPROFOR observers whose role was really to be observer more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 302 could be provided to the witness, please. This is an ECMM teletype on the subject of HV involvement in BiH. (Handed). Let me ask you, first: when did you first see this document, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on 18th June, because during that time period I was the head of the operations, so this communication was sent to the head of the operations and I was, indeed, head at that time, so I must have been the first of the persons to actually read this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the middle of paragraph 5, which reads, referring to General Praljak: "The general also acknowledged that HV troops are present inside Bosnia-Herzegovina along the cease-fire line, south-west of Trebinje, a fact already known to ECMM." Do you know where Trebinje was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps at that time I knew, but right now know, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it south-east of Mostar, the cease-fire line with the Serbs in Herzegovina, or you have no recollection? No recollection? If you could indicate "no" for the record, you are shaking your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would actually have to see the map to tell you exactly where it was, but right now, the name of that city means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The next sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you like for the witness to see the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, because I am sorry for interrupting you, but you seem to be drawing the conclusion that simply since the witness -- or the Colonel said he does not know, he did indeed say if he saw the map he could tell you. I do not want you prolonging these proceedings, but I do not want you to draw the conclusion, one way or the other. That is simply what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Ultimately the court will have a map and it will show where this city is, so I do not think it is necessary to take time in the cross-examination to further establish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The next sentence refers to sightings of personnel wearing HV uniforms in Central Bosnia. Was it of interest to ECMM whether there were HV troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed there were. Yes, we were asked to produce information to that effect in order, once and for all, to confirm -- or rather not to confirm the rumours that were circulating on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever observe any HV units in the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca or Kiseljak during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any reports -- reported sightings of such units in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist in providing a document to the witness. (Handed). If it could be marked as the next Defence exhibit in order, please. I believe that is 113.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, if you could look at the document. I am not going to ask you to read it unless you would like to read the whole thing. My question is simply: is this an ECMM report to RC Zenica prepared by your fellow Monitors during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is how we operated. A detachment would send a report and then later on, as the head of operation -- the head of operation would compile all these documents and also to share them with UNPROFOR and other organisations with which we had affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you recognise Mr. Friis-Peterson's signature in the upper right-hand corner of the first page of the document? It is the upper right-hand corner of the first page, I am indicating, if you are having trouble finding it, where I am pointing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see the place, but in my presence, Mr. Friis-Peterson never signed anything. The documents were sent by pouch, and so simply at that time it seems that Mr. Friis-Peterson was in that Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have one more document to provide to the witness, Mr. President, if the usher could assist. This, I believe, will be Defence 114. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you finished with document 213 or is this 214 you are basing your question on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am done with 213 for now, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does this also appear to be an ECMM teletype you would have received as operations officer of the Regional Centre Zenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, with respect to paragraph 4, do you have any recollection of receiving this report of a Joint Operational Centre meeting, which, among other things -- and I am referring to bullet points 3, 4 and 5 now -- in which agreement was reached on a safe corridor to all Vitez, that is bullet point number 3; agreement was reached on clear orders given to clear the AOR (Area of Responsibility) from snipers, that is bullet point number 4; lastly, release of all prisoners, except from criminals, point number 5? Do you have any recollection of receiving that information at approximately this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I say "yes", this is absolutely the report that I received and the decisions that were made. Yes, they were in conformity with the rules, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You can put that exhibit aside. I am done with it. You said yesterday that "people in positions of authority" -- this is page 14 of the draft transcript of yesterday's proceedings -- "did not do everything they could in order to prevent the loss of life in Central Bosnia". When you say: "persons in positions of responsibility did not do everything they could to prevent loss of life", are you intending to reference any particular standard of conduct, be it a moral standard or a standard that may be embodied in the Canadian Armed Forces Handbook, or a standard found elsewhere, or are you simply speaking from a personal standpoint; your own personal moral conviction is the standard that you are referring to when you make the statement I referenced? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite simple, I served with the NATO forces; I also served with the American forces, and I am a career officer, who has also been trained as an intelligence officer so I am very aware of the military procedures in the Soviet Union at the time. What I can tell you is that all commanders must be in a position to be able to assure his command, and also to take appropriate measures to ensure that his command has been carried out. I also stated here in this courtroom that I did not expect for any crimes to be committed. That is not what I was saying. What I was saying, to my memory, I do not remember seeing any concrete steps taken to limit the actions which were committed either by out of control soldiers or by units within their control. This is what I expected to see. During the period in which I was there, there were several incidents which should have been brought to the local HVO authorities and we, indeed, reported to them. These should have been clues to them and enough to realise there had been some break in the chain of command and that someone had not done there job. So some action should have been taken and perhaps some action of the commander of Busovaca, who seemed to be disobeying his orders or taking his orders from another commander. I expected this commander to continue to assume his authority and to demonstrate that he is, indeed, the ultimate commander of that area, or at least to go there and reprimand this man or at least to change the command there. I did not see this type of action taken by the authorities in the presence of the HVO -- HVO authorities. So, I am saying this has nothing to do with what army you are in. This is a military type of order and that a commander is responsible for its troops and for the actions of his troops. So, the commander is ultimately responsible for all the actions of his men. This is the only way, in my mind, that one can truly defend oneself before a court of law, that one can say that one has taken simple steps in order to prevent such a situation from occurring. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than what you have just said, are you referencing any particular standard of national law, international law, or from any other source, other than a standard which is within yourself as a result of your training and professional experience and which you have articulated very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
