utterances.text: I am sorry, it seems to me that the witness has answered this question. He has answered this question. He stated that what he said was his personal opinion, no matter what army one belonged to. So, please do not ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will not, your Honour. The question is: is it a standard within, or is it one thought, if so, where is it taught --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, not at all. No, Mr. Hayman, he has already answered quite well to that question. I am not going to say "very well", as far as relevance, I am saying that he responded very exactly to the question you asked. He said he has a knowledge of other armies and that he is familiar with the actions and he said he feels there are certain rules which should govern all commanders. So please go on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prior to reaching this opinion, as to Colonel Blaskic, have you seen the reports or obtained information concerning the reports that he received from subordinates concerning events during the war in Central Bosnia? Have you had access to that material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially -- I simply reiterate -- that I never mentioned the name of Colonel Blaskic. I mentioned authorities responsible for the HVO. Secondly, if this report was submitted to me, I would have been in a position -- in a much more credible manner to assess the actions taken by the HVO authorities and to see whether or not there were any problems linked to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you agree those reports would be very important in determining and judging the acts of a commander; what information did the commander receive; correct? That is very important information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not really relevant to see whether or not there is something written on a piece of paper. A piece of paper means nothing. What is important is to see whether or not in the field there were actions that were taken and which were applied and whether or not a different type of behaviour took place. This was a war of paper, we received a lot of different protests from the left and from the right with perhaps good or perhaps poor intentions. It is one thing to have good intentions, another thing is to actually apply them. I am telling you that I could not see anything that would lead me to believe that one was making an effort to try to maintain a true sense of command in the chain of command within all the troops. If that did take place, very well, but I did not see this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree that the information a commander receives is important to the commander's ability to react and respond appropriately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do understand what you want, in the way of a response. If you want to know whether or not a commander needs information or not to act, of course, yes. A commander must be able to have trust that the information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, wait a minute. I am sorry. I think that Mr. Hayman asked you a question. He has asked you twice because you have not responded to the question. You did not respond the first time, whether or not, in your opinion, the knowledge -- objective knowledge of some documents would then enable one to determine the actions of a chief. This is the question. Please respond to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but my lack of comprehension, I do not understand the question, the nature of the question. I can answer "yes" or "no".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Hayman, go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than what you may have in your private archive, have you obtained access to the other orders issued by the accused, some of which are already in evidence in this case? Did the Prosecutor make those materials available to you so that you could see for yourself what steps Colonel Blaskic did take during the conflict or have you not had access to that body of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the only documents I consulted were the documents I was able to see, either documents which came from the Zagreb headquarters or those sent from all the detachments which came from all the UN troops, the UNPROFOR troops, who were -- which were sent to us or which were sent to us in one way or another. That is all the ones I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If an HVO order was not sent to the ECMM, is it safe to presume you did not see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said yesterday that a commander has the responsibility, in your opinion, to establish a system for gathering information and disseminating orders. Would you agree that that includes setting up a headquarters staff, composed or comprised of the best people available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hesitate to answer, Mr. President, because the term "competent".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Defence, would you please clarify your question, because the term used "competent" could be vague?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I did not use the term "competent", so there has been a mistranslation. Would you agree that setting up the type of system I referenced includes setting up a headquarters staff composed of the best people available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, naturally you are going to take the best people available for your headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then it is the duty of the commander to have regular meetings, regular interaction and communications with that staff so that the staff is used effectively; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. In fact, that is why you have a head of the headquarters, who is in charge of working on a regular basis with the staff and then to be able to go to visit the troops in the field. There should be then a link between the head of the headquarters and the commander and they should have regular meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is also the responsibility of a commander, is it not, to communicate clearly with that staff and other subordinates, including at times in writing, so that directions are clear; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Not in agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I said I am completely in agreement. I am in agreement with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please try to put your questions more directly, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. I am not sure what the problem was on that last exchange. Can you tell us, Lieutenant-Colonel -- and I am -- Mr. President, I am nearing the conclusion, I have one more area of inquiry. Can you tell us: the HVO soldiers in the Lasva Valley, were they housed in barracks or did they live in their own homes and were they dispersed in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were in barracks and others lived in various buildings which were -- various areas on the line of -- on the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where were the barracks in the Lasva Valley, housing HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never invited to visit them. There were some in Vitez, some in Busovaca and some in Kiseljak, that is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At times when you were serving on the Busovaca Joint Commission, did you and General Merdan and Mr. Nakic go to the front-line so that Merdan or Nakic could communicate directly or talk to the local commanders at the front-line and urge them to obey cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that necessary because, in this particular theatre, there was great difficulty in obtaining respect and adherence to cease-fire orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was how the Commission worked. No action was carried out alone or only with the HVO or only with the Bosnians. You should know that the Commission had to be sure that there were some agreement on the cease-fire and that this was indeed carried out. This was the main mission of the Commission, to go into the field and to investigate and confirm that it was being applied. So, at that time period, these kind of visits had two purposes: for those troops which were isolated it enabled the other camp to send on information and orders. For the other troops which were not as isolated from the chain of command, while this enabled the commanders then to have a visit and also to make sure that everything was moving in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that, at the level of foot soldiers, the war in Bosnia was mainly fought by civilians; would you agree with that proposition? It is page 319, "Broken Lives", Lieutenant-Colonel Bob Stewart. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My own research seems to tell me not the contrary, but rather it was a little more ambiguous than that. I can tell you that in -- under the Tito regime that nearly all the civilians were called upon to enlist and to do some military service at one point or another. So, it is for this reason that the majority of the civilians did, indeed, have HVO -- or rather had Yugoslavian uniforms. That is why at one point I said that as far as -- in confirming one person is from one army or another, would depend on one's identity cards and the identity they had on their shoulders. What I can say is that there was a bit of all of this, there were civilians, yes, I saw them, and there were also other young people who seemed to have carried out some military training, then there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever commanded a military unit in combat yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never commanded any military troops in a time of combat, but I have commanded the ECMM in Zenica during the time at which we were, indeed, under mortar fire and under artillery fire. I think this experience, perhaps, it can be significant to say, yes, I have been under that experience. There was a baptism of fire, because during that time period I was responsible for evacuations or to explaining whether or not we would go from point A or point B. Indeed, I was responsible for the evacuation of Travnik, even though it was under fire at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On 18th April 1993, or thereabouts, you concluded that Franjo Nakic had been demoted from the position of deputy commander to the position of chief of staff, HVO Operative Zone Central Bosnia; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I said, on 18th April, this is in my notes, is that Mr. Nakic was no longer the commander, but later on when the new Joint Commission was established it was at this time that I saw Mr. Nakic reappear as head of operations. In the central zone, the Central Operational Zone of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So that the terms are perfectly clear -- because they are being translated back to me in something less than the terminology that I think is the specific terminology here. Prior to 16th April 1993, did you believe Franjo Nakic to be the deputy commander of the HVO, Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of the documents at the time were signed, showed Mr. Nakic was the deputy commander. Indeed, I saw a document from 13th February indicating he was the deputy commander or at least as an individual representing Colonel Blaskic, as a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the conflict, be it the 16th or 18th or 20th April, you concluded that Mr. Nakic was no longer the deputy commander, but was the Chief of staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once again, based on the documents which show the joint command at that time, indeed, at that time it showed he was the deputy commander of this camp and then also that Mr. Nakic was no longer the deputy commander and that he was, instead, head -- or chief of staff of the unit of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that particularly significant from a military perspective, because a deputy commander is in the chain of command and has command over the body of troops within that element or body of organisation, whereas a chief of staff does not have direct command over the forces? If not, what is your understanding of the distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not quite the way -- it is not quite the way you said it. In the armies I am familiar with, perhaps it was different in Bosnia, but in the armies I know, the deputy commander is the person who is designated in order to replace the commander if anything should happen to him. Among other things, when the commander must be away for rather long periods, it would be the deputy commander who takes control of the operations. However, the Chief of Operations, even if it is not specifically command of an operational unit, he is the one who commands the headquarters on that level of the formation. If you are looking at an army corps, you will see there was a general who was going to act as a Chief of Operations and that general will command all the staff working within those headquarters, so that he can apply the directives which have been issued by the commander when he was not there and would not be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you conclude that this change in Mr. Nakic's status was a demotion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I conclude is that Mr. Nakic was no longer Colonel Blaskic's replacement when he was not there. In addition, I concluded -- I could not explain the reason why he was given the title of Chief of Operations or the person responsible for the headquarters, because he was no longer in the headquarters. Therefore, the conclusion that I drew was that he had been given some type of title and that he was not really in authority, in a position to do anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So, you concluded he had been pushed aside, in substance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically that. I would just like to repeat here, something which is very important: it is not only my opinion, I tell you again that all of the reports that were drafted by the Zenica headquarters according to what I have -- were not only my opinion but of the regional Zenica command, so those -- even if I were to write something had been done under the authority that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have said you drew these conclusions from documents. Did Mr. Nakic or anyone else in the HVO tell you that his position had changed from deputy commander to chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I said that the first time it appeared was on the documents that had been signed, the documents dated 13th February, which describe Mr. Nakic as being the deputy commander and which implement the Operative Zone or the joint -- where the Joint Commander says that he was the Chief of staff. This is a document signed by Hadzihuseinovic and by Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Putting documents aside, did Nakic or anyone else in the HVO tell you, did you have a discussion or conversation with them in which they told you that: "Nakic has been pushed aside, he is no longer the deputy commander, he is the chief of staff"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember having had any specific discussion to that effect concerning Colonel Blaskic. The only thing -- I saw Mr. Nakic in the middle of that crisis, he was not there, he was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You went to see him at home. If the map could be replaced on the ELMO, can you tell us where his home was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember, I could do better than that. I have a photograph of myself with Mr. Nakic and his wife at their home. I can go get the photograph, then you can tell me exactly where -- where in the region he had his house. I do not remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That will not be necessary to do that, Lieutenant-Colonel. Do you remember, in going to his house, did you pass the BiH Army territory? In other words, was he cut off at his house on 18th April 1993 when you went to go see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. All that my notes says is that Mr. Nakic seems to have been removed from his position. The reason I reach that conclusion is that when you are in the midst of operations, ordinarily your place is not at home but your place is at headquarters and even at headquarters, there are rooms which allow staff to remain on site so they could work 24 hours a day. That is the approach that I used in order to realise that something had happened. You do not send your deputy commander to go sleep at home when he is in a combat area which could easily be cut off from your headquarters, but you keep him there, you keep him there at headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is the last thing you would expect if the commander expected a general conflagration and conflict, to send your deputy home to a location where he might be cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the commander who is responsible for things has to keep all the staff with him. That is what is ordinarily done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document, the contents of which are not particularly important for my purpose today, and ask you a few questions. You will see it is an HVO document. The date -- let me ask Mr. Nobilo to read -- the date is the line beginning "DANA" in the upper left-hand corner of the first page. Could you read that line, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 27th January 1993. "At 2255 hours".

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Stand by for a moment. Could you look at the second page, Lieutenant-Colonel? First let me ask: on a daily basis, did the Busovaca Joint Commission and later the Joint Operational Centre issue joint orders signed by General Merdan and by Mr. Nakic, on a daily basis, or was that only true during the Joint Operational Centre period, that they issued a daily, signed order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both deputy commanders throughout the Busovaca -- the Joint Busovaca Commission sessions did not sign things. They were simply there to investigate the application of the -- to investigate the implementation of the agreements of 13th February. When they would come back the following day, they would speak on behalf of their commanders and they would often have documents which had either been signed by staff from their headquarters or by their commander. But, I do not remember their having signed something together, jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise Mr. Nakic's signature on the second page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you I do not remember having seen his signature. I just do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Nobilo to read the title above "Franjo Nakic" on page 2, so we can get a translation of the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "Chief of staff, Franjo Nakic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have another document to show the witness, Mr. President. If it could be provided to him, and be marked as Defence 116. (Handed). This is a document, Lieutenant-Colonel, from your private archive; correct? Which we can determine has your signature, dated in August of 1996, in the lower right-hand portion of the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree this is the document that was created as a result of the meeting on 20th April 1993, which included the parties that signed it, giving birth to the Joint Operational Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, what we were trying to do was the same thing in the Mostar sector. That is why all those people were there. It was not only for Central Bosnia. We were also trying to have the same thing, that is to have a joint headquarters in the Mostar region, but I do know that we tried to have this type of joint headquarters so that we could reduce to a minimum the fighting between the two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 references, in its first line, the Vitez Joint Operational Centre; correct? Do you see that, on the first line of paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, in this document, you see paragraph 1, which speaks for itself. Paragraph 2 references a cease-fire. Paragraph 3, the second sentence, do you see the sentence which I will read so we have a translation: "This joint OC [Operational Centre] will be headed at its beginning by both deputy commanders ..." Then the sentence continues. Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that the protocol envisioned by ECMM for the Joint Operational Centre, that it would be headed by the deputies of Blaskic on one hand and Hadzihuseinovic on the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it does not say it. It says it was the deputy commanders who would eventually act.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the deputy commanders -- the ECMM protocol envisioned for the JOC was that the two deputy commanders would get together and kick the thing off; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. In our opinion, it was the logical follow-up to Busovaca, Joint Commission, that is where we had -- at that point we had the two deputy commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, ECMM intended the same protocol of two deputies serving in the Busovaca Joint Commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to be careful with the terms that you are using. The agreement was signed by General Morillon, by Ambassador Thebault and then by the two commanders of the corps that were there. It was not the -- only at the initiative of ECMM. The documents referred to negotiations between the different levels. What I conclude from this is that it was the intention of these people on site to have both of the joint commanders in order to give the proper credibility so that the joint commands would be credible and would be able to operate as they should.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you said "both of the joint commanders", do you mean the two deputy commanders, to have them together in the Joint Operational Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have one more document for the witness, Mr. President. If the usher could assist. (Handed). This, I believe, will be Exhibit D117. While that is being distributed, let me ask you, Lieutenant-Colonel, Exhibit D116, which is the joint agreement, is this an authentic document from your private archive?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This document, Lieutenant-Colonel, I can tell you -- insofar as I understand it, it is in the BSC language -- this is the first joint order issued by the Joint Operational Centre on April 22nd, 1993. Let me ask my colleague to read the title. Again, the contents are not so important for my present purpose. I would like my colleague to read the identification of the parties in the two corners at the top of the page, the title of the document, then the parties signing the document and their respective titles. Could you do that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the left-hand corner it says: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Commander of the Third Corps Zenica." Below that, we have in handwriting: "Bila", which is the place, "22nd April 1993". In the right-hand corner it says: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, the command of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone, advance post, Vitez." In the middle we have the heading of the document: "The first Joint Operation Centre of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." We are going on to the signatures now. On the left side we have the stamp of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Third Corps and the text says: "Deputy commander of the Third Corps, Dzemo Merdan." On the right side is the stamp of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, signed by deputy commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Franjo Nakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, would it surprise you to learn that Colonel Blaskic never had a deputy in his operational zone command; that Mr. Nakic, both before the 16th April and after the 16th April, was the Chief of staff of the operational zone, Central Bosnia and that references to him, as a deputy commander were made for purposes of ECMM protocol and the documents that were created that gave rise to the Busovaca Joint Commission and the Joint Operational Centre? Would it surprise you, sir, to learn those facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be very surprised, and for several reasons, one of which is that all people that I worked with within Zenica on the Busovaca Joint Commission, always said to me that Mr. Nakic was the deputy. Mr. Merdan never contested that. Secondly, all the documents -- and if the Tribunal wishes, I can show you -- that the United -- United Nations and UNPROFOR during that period -- as you know, UNPROFOR was trying to give informations for intelligence purposes in order to -- all of them show in their organisational charts that Mr. Nakic was the deputy commander of Colonel Blaskic. In addition to that, I have a very clear recollection of having had discussions with Merdan, who told me that further to that, Nakic was no longer the deputy commander, he was the Chief of operations. If Mr. Nakic had still been the chief of staff, well then somebody was demonstrating bad faith because I always called him the deputy commander. It was really somebody was showing bad faith and people would be trying to show me documents or make me say things that are not -- that have mistakes in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I offer Defence Exhibits 112, 113, 114, 115, 116 and 117. I have nothing further for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot see how Exhibits 115 and 117 are exhibits at all, since the witness has never seen these documents before. They are in a language which he does not understand and they have just been produced by the Defence. I do not think these can be exhibited into evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As things stand now, I do not think they can be tendered as evidence. They do not comply with the Trial Chamber's case law in respect of tendering of documents. Therefore, for the time being we will keep them in abeyance. We will not accept them yet and we will see what we will do later on in the discussions. Mr. Cayley, I suppose you want to exercise your right to re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Landry, I will not keep you too long, I will try to get through this as fast as I can. You will recall in cross-examination you were asked a number of questions about the briefing for new ECMM Monitors. Unless you require it in front of you, I will not place it in front of you because it will simply add to the time. In that document, Mr. Hayman questioned you about paragraph 27; paragraph 27 being the paragraph where it states that it is believed -- that is the HVO is believed to be controlled by the Croatian army from Zagreb. The HVO operates in two main areas. Now, am I right in saying that the word "believe" is there because it was thought to be true at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the language that one uses, one was not 100 per cent sure, but when you are like 80 or 90 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that subsequent to the production of this document in February of 1993, that further information was gathered about this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A particular document which I introduced, it is a document that you have provided to the Prosecutor, which Mr. Hayman selectively referred to, is a document of 18th June 1993, which is a report from headquarters ECMM, in which -- and I will summarise, and if you can confirm whether this is correct: "In a recent discussion with ECMM headquarters, Major General Praljak from the Croatian Ministry of Defence acknowledged that Croatia has provided military logistic support to the HVO but denies direct involvement by HV combat forces in the fighting in Central Bosnia." Was that evidence that was subsequently discovered and, indeed, was informed to all ECMM units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, you saw a logistics unit in Prozor, in Central Bosnia, an HV logistics unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When you talk about units, I saw personnel from those units in Prozor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you term a logistics unit a combat unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A logistics unit is not a combat unit, even if they can defend -- things set up as defence as part of the organisation, but it is not a combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you fight a war without a logistics unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Logistics units have strategic and logistical advantages without them you cannot deploy; you cannot resupply, you can do nothing with your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you believe that that logistics units that you saw in Prozor was supporting the HV in combat with the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I could deduce is that, in fact, there were decisions taken by the HV command in order to let those units move about in Bosnian territory in such a way that they would either support HV or HVO units, fighting in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, I am right in saying that subsequently a substantial amount of further evidence was discovered that indicated that HV units were supporting the HVO in their fighting in Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. The information we subsequently received revealed that there was fighting with HV troops or elements which supported the HVO offensives on the road that went from Mostar to Jablanica and Fojnica. This is why it was almost impossible, throughout that State, to move about in those areas and we were prevented from going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who are the HVO fighting in that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the reports that we received told us that there was fighting between the HVO and the Bosnian Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever see, moving on, organised HVO units out of control in the municipalities of Busovaca, Kiseljak and Vitez? I will repeat the question: in your time in Central Bosnia, did you ever see organised HVO units out of control in the municipalities of Busovaca, Kiseljak and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Out of control"? I am trying to listen as careful as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sure that you are tired. If you could repeat the question another way, Mr. Cayley, perhaps the witness would understand it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whilst you were in the municipalities -- your duties involved you going to the municipalities of Busovaca, Kiseljak and Vitez. Did you ever see organised units of the HVO out of control?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would object to the question as vague. Out of whose control? What does he mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see units that appeared to be acting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, ask your question in a different way, Mr. Cayley. The objection is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Landry, during your time in Central Bosnia, did you ever see, in the municipalities of Busovaca, Vitez or Kiseljak, military units of the HVO that apparently appeared to be acting at their own will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about certain incidents which said that there were troops acting in a way that was out of control, but in respect of civil war, there was nothing to say to me the HVO troops were not controlled -- that they were not answerable to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hayman asked you a large number of questions about supply routes in and out of Bosnia and whether or not they were controlled by the HVO or the BiH. A very simple question: you were there for a large period of time, from March of 1993 through to August of 1993; who was better supplied in Central Bosnia, the HVO or the BiH? When I say "better supplied", I am talking about weapons, ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think beyond the shadow of a doubt that from the beginning of the period until the end of June -- the beginning of June it was the HVO, because they had control over the roads, the main roads, that major road that brought in all supplies into Central Bosnia and Tuzla, that is why there was a Tuzla convoy because the supplies were not arriving where they were supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman introduced a subject to you and then actually closed it down before you were able to fully express yourself. That concerns the events in Travnik of 13th June 1993. Am I right in saying that the report that was prepared by Jean-Pierre Thebault on 13th June 1993, stated that the HVO, through massive propaganda, deliberately arranged for a massive exodus of Croats from Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the information that we had at that time and which moved Mr. Thebault in giving much more weight to the headquarters by under-scoring that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let us speak about the events at the Kaonik camp, the imprisoned foreign Muslim nationals. Did the HVO ever tell you that the Busovaca Joint Commission, that there were a number of foreign nationals being held at Kaonik pending criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the BiH troops who told us in early March that there were foreigners, foreign nationals. I think also two Bosnian drivers who had been arrested and who were in that prison. Later on -- which came much later on, perhaps around middle or end of March, we learned that there were foreign nationals who were arrested by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Army representatives ask, on a number of occasions, the Busovaca Joint Commission for the release of those foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember unfortunately only the two occasions, the two dates I mentioned to you, regarding the freeing of these people, but perhaps other things could have happened. But I remember those two in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will ask the question again, because I think you may have not got a proper translation. Do you recall whether representatives of the Bosnian Army asked the Busovaca Joint Commission of the HVO about the status of these people, actually asked for their release; the individuals that were imprisoned at Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember on two specific occasions where this was done, where protest was made and we asked the HVO -- Bosnia asked the HVO corps for some information about these foreign nationals and asked for them to be freed. I also recall that at some point in time we wanted to visit one of these detention centres but we were refused access. I also recall another occasion where some pressure was put on the Red Cross authorities to try to also put pressure on the HVO authorities to also give us access to these detention centres, but this is a very vague memory I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the HVO response to the request for the release of these Muslim nationals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot respond directly because I -- I cannot remember whether there was anything really official of freeing, or whether or not these prisoners were to be handed over to other members, whether they were to be evacuated. I cannot really remember -- I do not remember what answer we received, but all I can tell you is that the action which was taken was taken by the HVO and that the HVO were -- rather the action to be taken by the HVO did not really satisfy the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Hayman asked you a number of questions and showed you certain documents about events which occurred in January of 1993 in Busovaca. Where were you in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was serving in the HQ in the Libyan forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where is that located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In province of Quebec in a country called Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were present in March and April of 1993; who, in your view, started the conflict during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conflict initiated in March and April, or the conflict initiated in January, because the conflict initiated in January --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am referring specifically to the conflict initiated in the March/April period of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I told you was that all of the information we were receiving -- in this information there were many, many provocative incidents which came from the HVO and that in these incidents, there was violence that was committed, in which both sides committed such acts, using the weapons they had in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman asked you a number of questions about whether or not a commander is expected to -- or would expect to receive reports from his subordinates and would be expected to transmit reports to his subordinates. Is it not also expected of an army commander to actually go out into the field and visit his units to ensure that they are properly incorporated within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, this is why there is a head of operations, and also a deputy commander so that he can be freed and therefore, he can ensure his authority is carried out and he can have this handed down to his subordinate. This is how a command is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A couple of final questions, Colonel: you are a lieutenant-colonel, do you have colleagues of your age who are now generals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least two colleagues of my class who became brigadier-generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What, in your view, are the qualities that are required of a colonel to be promoted to the rank of a general?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope of cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The objection is sustained. Please go on to another question, counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, you are going to receive some questions from the judges. This one is from Judge Riad. Judge Riad, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Hello, Colonel Landry. I have a number of questions for you. First of all, let us be very clear. I would like to have some instances clarified even further. I have before me here an order coming from General Blaskic, from 18th April 1993 in Vitez. It is only in English, I was not able to obtain this document in French, so I will read it in English. This is paragraph 4, which orders: "Gather the relevant data about the actors of the conflict, the causes of banishing people, murdering civilians and soldiers, burning houses and other buildings." Actually, what he is doing here is ordering to get hold of the authors or the perpetrators of these atrocities. Now, to your knowledge, when were these orders carried out and what happened to these orders? Were there measures carried out? Were there any actions taken against the perpetrators, did they look for these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my memory I cannot remember, your Honour, any reports that came subsequently that would confirm that the perpetrators of these crimes were arrested or whether any investigation was carried out by the HVO authorities to try to learn what had happened. To the best of my knowledge, I do not remember having seen any report to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I will also ask you whether or not you can clarify some of the issues, the fact that there was nothing said. Earlier you stated that the HVO did not give any assistance regarding the investigations in the Ahmici village and also in Vitez and that no report was submitted to the Commission, if I understand what you stated correctly. Now, this absence of presence of any reports, would you say that was a position, or would indicate the position of the HVO towards your Commission, indicating they did not wish to cooperate, or would you fear that perhaps -- would you think rather it was only about the incidents of the Ahmici village and also Vitez that they were decided not coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some reports in the month of March and April. In fact, I reported in the month of March that I felt that things were going well and that both sides were cooperating in that they were able to implement this cease-fire agreement. But, from the month of April, principally in the early part of the month of April, we had the feeling, or I had the feeling and my colleagues that, on the HVO side, it seems they were looking for any excuse they could find not to cooperate, while on the Bosnian side they seemed to be always ready to cooperate and to assist us. You talked about the Ahmici incidents; I can also mention other incidents in which -- there were incidents committed in the Kiseljak area. I can also refer you to reports in which Canadian troops which were accompanying investigators for the ECMM were fired upon by HVO troops. They did not want for us to be able to move on our own to be able to investigate these allegations of crimes that were allegedly committed. So, once again, I must say that from my own memory of what happened in this field, it was never the case with the Bosnians. They were always with us or at least with me when we carried out our investigations. So we did not really have the same type of support or the same willingness to offer resources to carry out such reports or these investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you try to learn why? Which conclusion did you draw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the conclusion I have drawn is that, indeed, they did not want to cooperate. They did not want to cooperate completely with the members of the ECMM in order to put an end to this practice which is being carried out. That is the conclusion I have drawn, as well as the conclusions of my colleagues; that there was some effort -- rather, there was not a very open attitude on their behalf, which is different from the other side. It seems that they always wanted to push things back, to delay and delay, and restricting people from being able to move about, to such a point that our head of Mission told us in one of his reports that 10,000 civilian Croats were forced to leave the Travnik area, so that they can control the area and make sure that the HVO had a better position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. Perhaps you were seen very poorly then, as a sort of obstacle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke of a mock execution which was carried out in Skradno; do you recall? You said that there was a mock execution that was being carried out. Were there riots in Skradno that would justify this type of terror?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the people I am referring to were two women, in particular, with children, who came crying and told me what had happened to them. I could not understand the reasons for these type of gestures, even to the point at which I learned later on, during other visits, that when these people tried to leave Skradno village, they had to sign a paper saying that they were doing so on their own free will and that these people were displaced persons who were living in the sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Are you saying they did not do this freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you say "not doing it freely" what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are saying that they do not leave freely, on their own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because they had to sign a document saying they left the village and they had to leave their goods, but they had do so without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are saying then they had to leave -- not of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I am saying to you, your Honour, is that equipment was being stolen, their vehicles were being stolen, life was being made very difficult for them, even at the hospital in Busovaca, so it seems that they were being told: "If you wish to be treated in a better manner, then go to Zenica, there the Muslims will take care of you. In the meantime, if you do that, we will make sure that we can use your house and perhaps take possession of this house for our people". Later on a report was submitted and I saw this later on in which people were forced, Muslims who had been displaced, they were forced to leave Skradno and this was organised and, indeed, I was in the field when this was organised and they organised buses and all the displaced persons who were occupying houses were Muslims from Zenica, were quite simply forced to leave this housing, even though they were there for six months. That way, other displaced persons from HVO were able then to take possession of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to ask you a question about Rotilj. It was HOS, you said HOS had created this tragedy by burning the houses, et cetera. I would like to know whether this HOS was a dissident of the HVO or adversary of the HVO; what is this HOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are two views on this: either HOS was the dissident of the HVO who were committing crimes so that they could not be recognised. Perhaps they are wearing hoods. Another theory is that HOS was quite simply an extension of the elite troops which were being used in order to carry out an ethnic cleansing and also to create violent situations against the other ethnic group to force that ethnic group to do the same thing, then eventually to use the situation to show that the two communities could not live together. Then, eventually to force the Croatians who were living in the Bosnian zone to return to their Croatian zones. This I was able to experience myself during the entire summer-time, knowing that there were some 10,000 to 20,000 people in Zenica who were mainly families living there and to see on a regular basis pressure put upon them by the HVO, asking that these people leave Zenica to go back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, this HOS, no matter how one might see them, do you feel that they were able to be controlled by the HVO? Were they stronger than the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps they were stronger than the HVO. One thing is certain, that the number of incidents that were created or instigated by HOS tells me they definitely use much of the equipment that belonged to the HVO, either artillery ammunitions or weapons and munitions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are not very clear, you always talk about the command responsibility without talking about Colonel Blaskic, in particular. Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander at that point in time, it was Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He was the uncontested commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I am telling you is that as far as I know from all the documents I have and all the meetings I participated in, it was Blaskic who always presented himself as the commander of the HVO troops in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that when you arrived that Colonel Blaskic was captain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, what I stated was that what I was told was that Colonel Blaskic was once a captain in the Yugoslav army, while his equivalent is -- his counterpart was a colonel at that point. The two knew each other and that perhaps might explain why Hadzihuseinvoic had occasion to sit at the same table as his HVO counterpart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So let us say then he was a captain, then later on became colonel, then a general. You might -- you should also agree with me that this was a very fast promotion to that level; what were the reasons for this very quick rise to this rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that during the Second World War, these type of promotions happen quite commonly. If you have a lack of officers, then you will take your best members and you would put them in two command positions. I think that this was -- it had already been one year since the operations had been carried out in Bosnia -- on Bosnian soil. So I can assume, perhaps in a naive fashion, that the HVO headquarters in Mostar continued to maintain him in that post because he was someone doing a good job and he had the responsibility for all of the HVO forces in Central Bosnia and also all the equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So this is someone who has some control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either someone who is very intelligent who was good control or someone who has a very good knowledge of the military situation and has a good deal of clout. I say he has a very good knowledge of his men and also of the terrain because on several occasions I have said that some of this troops were in isolated area, so he must have a very good sense of his men and be able to assess the knowledge of his men and be able also to put them into very specific locations and then give them human and material resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: One last question: you also spoke about the presence of logistics and the Croatian forces, I think also you talked about Croatian logistics and also Croatian forces. From whom would these Croatians receive their orders? Would they receive them from the command -- in your opinion, the command that was the Bosnian command from the HVO and Colonel Blaskic, or would it, instead, come from the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must admit to you, your Honour, that the HV troops that I saw in Bosnia were not under the orders of Colonel Blaskic, but rather within the command zone which dealt with Herzegovina. All I can tell you is that I had good relations with the people dealing with -- later on, I can see that there were relations that were maintained, but I cannot -- it is difficult to say whether or not -- that in some places, it is difficult to say whether or not some troops, which are using some areas, were co-ordinated by the country which was lending these troops. So, I saw this, together with my colleagues, as strategy that was being established in which the Croatians were supporting certain missions or certain types of operations in Bosnian soil. This would be for their long-term plans that they may have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were saying this was to serve some sort of Croatian policy on a long-term basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Colonel, there were two sides in conflict; Croats and Muslims. There was the Busovaca Joint Commission. My impression is that the function of the Joint Commission was to try to defuse any military confrontation between the two sides; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, all the purpose, the Commission would deal with someone on each side. On the Croatian side, with whom would the Commission deal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the senior representative who was there at that time, Mr. Nakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: However you describe it, Mr. Nakic represented whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He represented -- I am sorry, he represented the commander of the central operational zone, that is to say, Colonel Blaskic at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you then deal with Colonel Blaskic in respect of all military incidents, including those involving the HOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not -- it was not my task. My task at hand at that time and where I could intervene was with the two deputy commanders. This was the authority I had. If we were to also intervene at a higher level, at that time it would be Ambassador Thebault who was to apprise us of the situation. Then, he was the one who was going to meet with Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question slightly: you, yourself, would not deal with Colonel Blaskic; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Commission would deal with him through Mr. Nakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding of the Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So all I am asking is this: when military incidents occurred which involved the HOS, would the Commission deal with Mr. Nakic or with Colonel Blaskic in relation to those incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, to the best of my knowledge, all of the protests, no matter whether or not they were committed by bandits or by the HOS or by HVO troops, were subjected to the Commission, all of the protests. It was the Commission then that, as I explained, would take action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The machinery of the Commission would ultimately involve reference to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now then, shall we move on to your testimony about statements made to you about the existence of a mass grave for Croats? I think it was in the vicinity of Zenica. Do you recall that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that part of my evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You, as in duty bound, went out to investigate, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to investigate those allegations, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I just want a little bit of clarification about something you may have said which may also have escaped my attention. Did your investigations turn up evidence about the existence of the mass grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was not able to find out exactly how many bodies there were. They did not dig them up in front of me. But with the Bosnian authorities, we were able to determine where the mass grave was located and with the authorities of the Red Cross later on, the incident was indicated in our daily reports, that is what we found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You mentioned the Bosnian authorities. Did they cooperate with you in respect of those investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I want to put things back into perspective, your Honour. This happened, if I am not mistaken, in July. At that point, the situation in Central Bosnia had completely changed. There were all types of allegations regarding violence against the Croats who had remained in Zenica. This -- regularly we would keep changing our attitude towards the Croats, sometimes we would be against the Croats, sometimes we would take negative positions against the Bosnian troops who committed certain actions. I remember I had gone to see the Bosnian authorities and I asked them to be able to go to investigate the allegation, and that I went there at that time with Father Stefan and there were also allegations in the same report according to which there had been desecration of a Croatian church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us turn briefly to the incidents which occurred at Ahmici. You have heard from learned counsel for the Defence of certain documents signed by Colonel Blaskic in relation to those events. Now, if Colonel Blaskic had, in fact, undertaken an investigation into those events, was that investigation something which was likely to come to your notice, either directly or through the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was starting at that point, that the Busovaca Joint Commission ceased to exist and was replaced by the joint headquarters. At that point I was moved from the Busovaca Commission to the Operational Centre. In all good faith, I have to tell you that if this type of report had been submitted to us at ECMM, I should have been made aware of it, and we would have talked about it on an every-day basis. I have to tell you that I have absolutely no memory of having seen that. That is a report from General Blaskic on the incidents at Ahmici. To the contrary, I saw other reports from a special committee that was done later, by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I am not talking about reports now. I am asking you this: if, in fact, he had instituted an investigation, would the fact of that investigation have come to your notice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it should have. I do not remember ever having seen one though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If, in fact, he had instituted an investigation into the events at Ahmici, would you have regarded that as a matter of importance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I have a last question for you, and it concerns your evidence about the evolution of relations between the two sides. As I understood you, you were saying that relations between the two sides were improving during March, but that, come early April, they started to deteriorate; is that a rough summary of your evidence on the point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So, the threshold point would have been represented by the first week of April; that is the threshold point in the dip in the quality of relations between the two sides, the change would have occurred sometime in the first week of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason that I am hesitating is that I am trying to remember the date when I tried to have -- together with the local commanders -- to have the trenches filled in. I think it must have been -- I would say, yes, it was more or less around the first week of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We are agreed after all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned the Vance-Owen Plan, which I think assigned province number 10 to the Croats. Do you remember your references to the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think you said that the Croatians were the first to sign on to the plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how I remember it, yes, that the Croats were the first who agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I take it you would accept that there is a difference between signing a plan and the implementation of the plan on the ground. You recognise the distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did any information ever come to your notice about an ultimatum or something in the nature of an ultimatum, having been issued by the Croatian side to the Muslim side requiring implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan by 15th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were on the ground, I was not given that type of information. The only thing that I can remember is I believe that the Muslims or Izetbegovic had signed the Vance-Owen Plan at the end of March or at least he had let it be understood that he had agreed with the implementation, or at least the principles of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very quickly, Colonel, because you have answered many questions of my colleagues: Ahmici. I did not really understand something; at one point you said there was no strategic objective. Then at another point in your testimony you said that there was a strategic objective. I did not grasp that. Perhaps you could clarify that conclusion for me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to tell you that I must have led you astray. When I spoke about strategic objectives I meant that militarily I did not see any reason for this kind of operation to be carried out, because as far as I knew it was not a military strong point for either side. Then later on, had it really been a strategic point it should have been maintained, troops should have been left there or at least positions should have been constructed in order to confront the other side. Perhaps it was in that perspective that I expressed myself poorly with the word "strategic" or "tactical".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One or two short additional questions. When you speak about uncontrolled or uncontrollable forces, have you heard of things like -- uncontrolled troops such as the Jokers -- the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I did some research, I saw those words were used, but the same thing was also in existence, that was the HOS -- the Muslims had the same -- had accounted for the HOS. They had the type of HOS stripes, they were the Mujehadeen amongst the Muslims who had insignia on their shoulders which would show a naked woman. I have a picture of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I did not quite understand what your answer was to the Defence counsel when he asked you whether, for a military authority -- a high-ranking military authority, in order to understand his authority he -- one must take into account all information and reports that came from his subordinates. I think the question that you were asked was to find out whether this type of information appeared important to you, and I think the word "crucial" was, in fact, used. I do not know whether you answered that. Could you specify that more clearly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is clearer for me in the way you have asked the question. Yes, indeed. It is an essential tool for any good military commander. It is good to give orders and have them executed, but one has to also know -- to get feedback, as we say in military talk, in order to adjust the troops or to whether we have to readjust our weak and strong points, we absolutely need feedback from information coming out of our advanced troops so that we might be able to have an influence over the outcome of the battle by taking the appropriate measures in order to counter or to respond to the information that one has received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talk about the Croatian units, the strategic ones, apparently, whose visible traces you found, in your opinion, were they there in respect of the previous conflict against the common enemy, which was Serbia, or did you have the impression from all the information sources that you received that their strategic objective had changed and that they were now following another policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that in the region that we saw them in Prozor -- it was difficult to understand that those Prozor troops were logistical and that they were in order to fight against the Serbs on the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke a great deal about the strategy; this kind of two-faced game, provocation, underhanded provocations in order to then give rise to a conflict, then to respond to the reprisals or to the responses of the Muslims. Then there was a kind of -- as opposed to a kind of image that one wanted to give out as ideally as possible before the international community. That was very clear in how you spoke. My last question is to know whether this opinion is a strictly personal one, or is it an opinion that was carried along by UNPROFOR, by the politicians? I am not asking -- talking about indirect testimony, I am just asking about whether this was a personal opinion mostly, or a rather widespread opinion held among political and military authorities at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to tell you very clearly that this was the opinion that was shared at that time by all of the ECMM officials and which was also shared by the UNPROFOR headquarters. I would tell you that even if it was shared, there was a hesitation, a reluctance to say it, because you did not have all the details to confirm what had happened -- you needed more details to confirm it. But, I was in a position to give a more personal opinion, a more specific opinion in that respect. In fact, that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, if there are no further and additional questions, we have finished. You have given very, very substantive testimony to the Tribunal and the Tribunal needs witnesses who have strong convictions. The International Criminal Tribunal would like to thank you. You may now go back to your own country with the feeling of having done your duty, which is the principle according to which all high-ranking military people adhere. Do not move for the time being. We are going to end our work. Mr. Harman, we will resume tomorrow afternoon again, probably at 2.30. I think that we will not be able to beyond 5.30. The length of the questions asked, of course, will determine how far we can get and I know that you do not want the witness to come back on Monday, but all of us are serving the cause of justice, and if he has to come back on Monday, then he will come back on Monday. I was sensitive to the fact that this witness has already been displaced more than once. We will try to do everything we can in order for things to go as smoothly as possible tomorrow. I see Mr. Kehoe has stood up and has a comment he would like to make or a question he would like to ask. Mr. Kehoe, does it have to do with the schedule? Let me remind you that we have a meeting of the presiding judges of the Chambers tomorrow in the beginning of the afternoon. We hope to be finished by 2.30. I am not quite sure, I am not the one in charge of the meeting; it is the President of the Tribunal who is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President and your Honours. With regard to Mr. Vuilliamy, he has informed me that he has significant professional obligations that he has put off several times and has to go back to the United States on Sunday. He cannot hold over -- this is what he told me, he could not hold over until Monday, assuming we do not finish tomorrow afternoon. I will check with him and discuss it with him at some length to see if he can accommodate those plans, but he seemed to indicate to me that he could not. Possibly I will ask what plans we could settle to have him come back at another session to complete any cross-examination. At this point, Mr. President, I cannot tell you that, based on what he has told me, that he could come back on Monday. He has just had some serious professional problems -- concerns, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Are you more or less informed about the time he would take to give his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the story he will tell and, consistent with your Honours' opinion, it will be in a narrative form with very, very few questions on my part, it should be approximately two hours, two and-a-half hours or so. Depending on how quickly it goes, that is about how it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For things to be very clear, I do not want to give the impression that the judges are not available to the cause of justice, but please realise that I have commitments outside the Netherlands and that I have cancelled them tomorrow. I have a plane that leaves at 10.30 in the evening. This does not mortgage tomorrow's hearing, but as we all know, one has to go to an airport in order to get an aeroplane. I have cancelled all my engagements for the afternoon, therefore they have been postponed until Saturday morning. Therefore, it is not be the judge who will be the source of any delay. I am simply asking that one take -- acquire the habit of asking a central question, when I said around 5.30, it is so that I have a way of getting to the airport, but I want things to be very, very clear. In any case, it is not the judges who are causing delays. As regards the witness, I do not think the judges are the ones either who are responsible for the fact that the witness who was in front of us has -- and whom we thank -- took more time than he initially would. Several weeks ago we agreed we would not limit the testimony time of the witness, in fact, I brought up that question. I think we all agreed and said that this would not be done in this Trial Chamber, that is to limit the number of days for a witness. From that point on, I cannot say anything further. My colleague judges will have to come back as well. Tomorrow we will have more or less a regular day, a normal afternoon. Perhaps we should have begun Mr. Vulliamy's testimony today. Colonel Landry had many things to say and the cross-examination was also very detailed and very useful. Therefore, everyone is doing his best, but I think things have to be very clear. I cancelled all my appointments for tomorrow afternoon in a neighbouring country in order to allow the witness to testify. I am not the master of the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination and we will do what we can. If Mr. Vulliamy has to come back a third time, he will, but it will be another time, it will not be Monday. I simply say that we all understand the rules of the game. We understand we are in a legal system where ordinarily, except for special occasions, a witness should be able to be heard in three hours. This is an old discussion. If you think that this cannot be done, very well. This is not the judge who can impose another rule on you and will not do so. In that case, the witness would simply have to come back. I think things are clear now. Once again, the Tribunal thanks Colonel Landry. The court stands adjourned and we will resume tomorrow at 2.30 pm. (6.45 pm)
